[runtime] 2023-10-02 16:03:50 [verbose]: osu.Game.Rulesets.Osu.Objects.SliderRepeat @ 47089.64705239558 judged as LargeTickHit (simulating = False)

Large ticks affect combo, small ticks do not. Because the combo portion of "score V2" contains a sort of combo feedback (by incorporating `ComboAfterJudgement + 1` into the formula), judging the non-combo-affecting tail circle before the combo-affecting slider repeat _decreases the value of the slider tail_, as it doesn't get the extra 1 combo it would if the tail circle was judged after the repeat.

Possible solutions:

- When simulating autoplay, reorder judgements such that tail circles are judged as early as possible (fixes the immediate issue, but may cause score to get..... weird - stuff like doing things to hit a slider tail _late_ etc)
- Do not allow the slider tail to be judged before the last repeat.

> Possible solutions:
> 
> * When simulating autoplay, reorder judgements such that tail circles are judged as early as possible (fixes the immediate issue, but may cause score to get..... weird - stuff like doing things to hit a slider tail _late_ etc)
> * Do not allow the slider tail to be judged before the last repeat.

I think the second makes sense, to the point I naively assumed that was already the case (but I guess not).

Personally I'd have the assumption that nested hit objects are always judged sequentially. Wonder if it's too late to enforce this? Discussing with @smoogipoo I think we both agree on this one.

Will see what I can come up with.

The changes are still larger than I expected... 17% pp losses on one beatmap. It's worth checking to make sure of the cause here.

As discussed, the current theory is that these are sliders where there's a normal tick after the "last tick". Thinking about it a bit more, `master` may be correct here, and I question whether this PR is handling things correctly at all, because I'm fairly certain osu!stable doesn't discriminate between ticks - it only gets the next tick (by time) and only if it's the last tick (by time) in the list does it apply a special judgement (see https://github.com/peppy/osu-stable-reference/blob/master/osu!/GameplayElements/HitObjects/Osu/SliderOsu.cs#L2039-L2044 ). In this case, this would mean that if the "last tick" is -36ms and a tick is generated at -12ms, then the "leniency" is only 12ms.

Basically what I'm saying is this needs to be gone through with a fine comb. I haven't gone through this PR yet.

Keep in mind that this PR *changes the game behaviour* to be something completely different from stable, so I would expect changes. As in we're not going to end up with a zero-change spreadsheet.

I'll go through the largest changes and provide analysis on what is causing them, regardless.

Taking a moment to address the SR changes found in the spreadsheet on 5 beatmaps, I've looked into the [beatmap](https://osu.ppy.sh/beatmapsets/881996#osu/1844019) with the largest change in SR. We come across sliders like this:

00:57:383 (1,2,3,4,5) - 

![osu! 2023-10-04 at 05 15 11](https://github.com/ppy/osu/assets/191335/1371d31a-a2bc-43b6-8486-628529f16b36)

Taking the first of these sliders as an example, the length of the slider is 43 ms, which will trigger the "lesser lenience" as explained in the [updated comments](https://github.com/peppy/osu/commit/cfb18e18c060f4270925b544fa545518ac48dea6) with quite some detail. The lenience will thus be 21.5 ms, occurring halfway on the slider's path:

![osu! 2023-10-04 at 05 16 52](https://github.com/ppy/osu/assets/191335/185d1e5d-8730-45fd-8ff3-1b2c5ee13503)

If we adjust the follow circle to show where the "actual" follow region is by removing its animation, it looks like this:

![osu! 2023-10-04 at 05 19 30](https://github.com/ppy/osu/assets/191335/f88de469-bad5-4499-8fb0-da4361ea72e8)

With the new changes, the lenience would still be 36 ms, meaning the user only needs to hold until 7 ms into the slider. Visually:

![osu! 2023-10-04 at 05 22 28](https://github.com/ppy/osu/assets/191335/a3efd150-f63a-42f2-a2a3-df20ad129ab8)

Both cases should **not require positional mouse movement by the user**, so you may wonder why difficulty calculation (which is supposed to take minimum movement requirements into consideration) is different. That's where we check the diffcalc code and find it doesn't use the full `2.4f` tracking radius of the follow circle, but a reduced `1.8f`:

https://github.com/ppy/osu/blob/8d919912149a4853120612b67944492c27baa611/osu.Game.Rulesets.Osu/Difficulty/Preprocessing/OsuDifficultyHitObject.cs#L25

This is how things look with stable-style-lenience at `1.8f`. Note that the follow circle now no longer overlaps the starting circle and *does* imply user mouse movement requirements:

![osu! 2023-10-04 at 05 25 52](https://github.com/ppy/osu/assets/191335/57b10b64-0e60-49b1-9469-1b6438e0e50a)

So it's arguable whether this is something that needs to be resolved here. Here's some points:

- In the cited beatmap, users are unlikely to move their mouse (since they don't need to), so in actual fact the diffcalc on `master` using the `1.8f` scaled follow circle is likely less accurate
- If we are considering backporting the changes in this branch to stable, we'll want diffcalc to match the new behaviour.

I'll add isolated diffcalc test coverage with this specific slider for anyone who wants to play along at home.

The previous diff was wrong, because it turns out that in the previous code, the last normal tick could come *after* the legacyLastTick, resulting in the `[^1]` operation coming upon the later last tick. This is more correctly:

```diff

+++ b/osu.Game.Rulesets.Osu/Difficulty/Preprocessing/OsuDifficultyHitObject.cs
@@ -215,13 +215,20 @@ private void computeSliderCursorPosition(Slider slider)
             if (slider.LazyEndPosition != null)
                 return;
 
-            double trackingEndTime = Math.Max(
-                // SliderTailCircle always occurs at the final end time of the slider, but the player only needs to hold until within a lenience before it.
-                slider.NestedHitObjects.OfType<SliderTailCircle>().Single().StartTime + SliderEventGenerator.TAIL_LENIENCY,
-                // There's an edge case where one or more ticks/repeats fall within that leniency range.
-                // In such a case, the player needs to track until the final tick or repeat.
-                slider.NestedHitObjects.LastOrDefault(n => n is not SliderTailCircle)?.StartTime ?? double.MinValue
-            );
+            // This commented version is actually correct by the new lazer implementation, but intentionally held back from
+            // difficulty calculator to preserve known behaviour.
+            // double trackingEndTime = Math.Max(
+            //     // SliderTailCircle always occurs at the final end time of the slider, but the player only needs to hold until within a lenience before it.
+            //     slider.Duration + SliderEventGenerator.TAIL_LENIENCY,
+            //     // There's an edge case where one or more ticks/repeats fall within that leniency range.
+            //     // In such a case, the player needs to track until the final tick or repeat.
+            //     slider.NestedHitObjects.LastOrDefault(n => n is not SliderTailCircle)?.StartTime ?? double.MinValue
+            // );
+
+            double trackingEndTime = Math.Max(Math.Max(
+                slider.StartTime + slider.Duration + SliderEventGenerator.TAIL_LENIENCY,
+                slider.StartTime + slider.Duration / 2
+            ), slider.NestedHitObjects.OfType<SliderTick>().Last().StartTime);
 
             slider.LazyTravelTime = trackingEndTime - slider.StartTime;
 

```

This reduces the gap, and I've confirmed that `trackingEndTime` matches 1:1 with `master`. The remaining difference is due to the `for` loop just below this code, which is no longer getting tossed around by the `LegacyLastTick` and `LastTick` being mis-ordered and causing backward movement.

issue_context.title: `LegacyLastTick` is still being used for gameplay and editor displays
issue_context.body:
I'm not sure if we want this from a game mechanic perspective, but it's probably something worth noting until we discuss / finalise things.

https://github.com/ppy/osu/blob/f060e6a780c43057eea6cab2e140c8b6ca8da26e/osu.Game.Rulesets.Osu/Objects/Slider.cs#L196-L207

Noticed this while looking at https://github.com/ppy/osu/discussions/22726.
comments:
I'm not really even sure what's to discuss in this one. Seems like the spark here was an editor bug caused by using the legacy last tick's end time for the editor marker, but I'm not sure what else this issue encompasses beyond that?

We're working around `LegacyLastTick` in several places already:

https://github.com/ppy/osu/blob/36ebdd8d30130276d59a1268d85af28b17935324/osu.Game.Rulesets.Osu/Objects/Drawables/DrawableSlider.cs#L290-L293
https://github.com/ppy/osu/blob/36ebdd8d30130276d59a1268d85af28b17935324/osu.Game.Rulesets.Osu/Mods/OsuModSynesthesia.cs#L39-L44

and this comment seems to imply that the thing is largely there for diffcalc purposes:

https://github.com/ppy/osu/blob/36ebdd8d30130276d59a1268d85af28b17935324/osu.Game/Rulesets/Objects/SliderEventGenerator.cs#L69-L75

so what even would need to happen to progress this? Would one have to try and nuke that from the face of the earth and see what gameplay/difficulty implications this has?

The issue I see is that `SliderTailCircle` has become the new `LegacyLastTick`. It's holding a non-correct end time for sliders which could easily be used without realising (as has been in the editor in the issue that spurred the creation of this issue).

The discussion that needs to happen is whether we want this to continue to exist into the future, or whether it should
- Be confined to classic mod, removed from everywhere else (seems better but no idea how the implementation would look)
- Be confined to old beatmap versions (meaning beatmaps made after some point won't have the offset). Would be nice to fix this for new maps, but backwards compatibility is likely going to be an issue. And I have no idea (and don't really want to find out) if the 36ms offset is still required in stable for things to work correctly.

When this was implemented classic mod didn't even exist, so maybe it can be moved into a very localised implementation there?

Hmm. That's probably one to bounce off players and mappers alike, then.

We'll probably have to make this problem digestible to them somehow and concoct a less technical description, but it seems like it affects both playability and mapper agency.
Potentially.  The 36ms does mean that you can release sliders before they visibly end. If players prefer this then we may have to stick to it.

Yeah. Probably affects "tech" maps or whatever. There's also that weird part that on very fast sliders it is not 36ms but the dead center of the slider (start + end time / 2).

Relevant thing: https://github.com/ppy/osu-stable-issues/issues/808

I didn't realise this was a thing in stable, but this would have a huge impact on difficulty if removed indeed since all players subconsciously learned to use that leniency. 36ms seems arbitrary, but it does make sense to allow the player to exit (and stop holding) the slider-end within the 300s leniency at the very minimum (and 36ms is reasonable), since there's no reason to allow a player to be early on hit-circles and slider-heads but not on slider-ends (and slider-ticks ?). The "follow-circle" radius being bigger than the visual radius of slider-ends (and slider-track) was partially addressing the issue (only for the aim part) but doesn't work well for fast sliders because the follow-circle size doesn't scale with the speed.

I would take it further and say it could make sense to even allow the player to reach that slider-end late too, effectively providing a timing leniency window to slider-ends, and also extending this behaviour to slider-ticks since there's not much reason to treat them differently. Having a timing leniency window on slider-ticks would reduce the feeling that a lot of players have that "fast-slider maps are random" and make it less necessary to "cheese" such sliders by snapping the slider-ticks directly and not following the track at all. This has the opposite "problem" of potentially making slider-maps slightly easier than originally designed to be. I'd love to see what the community thinks of this.

In any case, my main point is this LegacyLastTick should remain, even for newer maps, unless an alternative leniency mechanic that allows for the same or more leniency is implemented instead.
BUT, if mappers want to have sliders that forces you to reach the slider-end without allowing for any "spacial"-leniency, then a new object-type should be created: that object would provide a visual hint of the "effective slider-end radius" with a different slider-end skin that is the same size as the follow-circle, to make it clear that the user should aim and (why not) also release the key inside this circle, with the standard OD leniency on the release as in mania.

To add my comment while this is fresh, the 36ms 'last tick' isn't a form of leniency but is actually the time the slider end is determined to have been hit or not - for a lot of gimmicky slider maps where the slider is too fast to follow (but still has no ticks) this has made players have to find out where the sliderball would be 36ms before the actual end of the slider and aim at that position instead of the sliderend.

I haven't had time to discuss or form an opinion on this issue yet, but the opposing sides are "how it should work" vs "how it has always worked". Do players want sliders to work as they should do, or should esoteric gameplay knowledge play a part in whether you can play slider gimmick maps? I'll open this to people for discussion, likely not an easy resolution to reach.

I wouldn't call the LegacyLastTick a "hack" because it's original purpose makes sense: Basically, just like we allow the player to be a bit early or late on aiming and tapping circles through the hit-windows, it makes sense to also allow the players to be a bit early or late on aiming slider-ends and on the release of the key.

And for that purpose, the LegacyLastTick works well if the sliders have a "reasonable" speed because people will follow the track and as long as they follow well enough and don't release the key any earlier that the LegacyLastTick, they validate the slider-end.

But for fast sliders (often found on tech maps), players naturally "snap" the slider-ticks and slider-ends (As in the video of @Walavouchey above, even if that's a bit extreme there) to reduce the risk of missing, instead of following the track regularly.

Thus the LegacyLastTick should act as a leniency. This is why i believe the approach suggested above makes a lot of sense: It allows the player to play as before (following the track and leaving early), while also allowing to snap the slider-ends without issues, as well as any behavior "in between" those two.

Whether this should be back-ported to stable or not is another subject.

One alternative simpler solution could have been to only check that the players still holds the key on the LegacyLastTick, but actually only check the aim part (that the cursor is inside the follow-circle) at the timing of the slider-end. This would however have several bad consequences:
- All players would have to relearn how to aim slider-ends as they were previously intuitively leaving the slider-track early.
- This would make a lot of maps harder to play as players would have less time to go to the next object.
- Both points above would make people unhappy about the feel of the game, and would lead to lower osu! lazer adoption.

I'd argue there's a need for the specific sliderend leniency of the LegacyLastTick in the game because hitting circles/sliderheads works with timing windows, and by intuition there should be an early part to that window for the sliderend where you can move away from it and still have the game consider it a perfect play, just like you can hit a few milliseconds too early and still get a 300. The LegacyLastTick does punish you for aiming only towards the end of a slider without following the body, but it's not really a good solution to that either because you can aim directly for the LegacyLastTick itself if you've memorized its location; if punishing not following the sliderbody was a priority, it should be done in another way.

So - I'd prefer if the LegacyLastTick acted in such a way that if you held the slider within the range of its position and the sliderend it'd give you the perfect judgement for a sliderend, just like Walavouchey described. You may as well drop Legacy from the name too, since it'd no longer be a port from stable.

It took players multiple years to discover how the LegacyLastTick actually worked (until the 36ms incident) and it only really became public knowledge once mappers actually started pushing boundaries with slider speeds. Removing it and its leniency entirely is a terrible idea because it makes gameplay harder with no upside.

Having the leniency depend on OD (or its own setting?) would be super interesting; that'd require some serious playtesting though.
